claim: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a complex degenerative disease of the central nervous system.
source: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a complex degenerative disease of the central nervous system, and elucidating its pathogenesis remains challenging.
evidence: This is a definitional statement presented in the abstract of the manuscript.

claim: The study used the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) model as the major analysis method to perform hypothesis-free Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis.
source: In this study, we used the inverse-variance weighted (IVW) model as the major analysis method to perform hypothesis-free Mendelian randomization (MR) analysis on the data from MRC IEU OpenGWAS (18,097 exposure traits and 16 AD outcome traits), and conducted sensitivity analysis with six models, to assess the robustness of the IVW results, to identify various classes of risk or protective factors for AD, early-onset AD, and late-onset AD.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: The study generated 400,274 data entries in total.
source: We generated 400,274 data entries in total, among which the major analysis method of the IVW model consists of 73,129 records with 4840 exposure traits, which fall into 10 categories: Disease, Medical laboratory science, Imaging, Anthropometric, Treatment, Molecular trait, Gut microbiota, Past history, Family history, and Lifestyle trait.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data about the study results.

claim: The IVW model analysis consists of 73,129 records with 4840 exposure traits.

claim: AD can be divided into two types: early-onset AD (EOAD, age of onset ≤65 years) and late-onset AD (LOAD, age of onset >65 years).
source: It can be divided into two types: early-onset AD (EOAD, age of onset ≤65 years) and late-onset AD (LOAD, age of onset >65 years); the proportion of LOAD in patients with AD is approximately 95%, with LOAD having a stronger genetic predisposition than EOAD (Godyń et al., 2016; Ransohoff and El Khoury, 2015; Zou et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript provides a definition with supporting citations.

claim: The proportion of LOAD in patients with AD is approximately 95%.
source: It can be divided into two types: early-onset AD (EOAD, age of onset ≤65 years) and late-onset AD (LOAD, age of onset >65 years); the proportion of LOAD in patients with AD is approximately 95%, with LOAD having a stronger genetic predisposition than EOAD (Godyń et al., 2016; Ransohoff and El Khoury, 2015; Zou et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this statistical claim.

claim: LOAD has a stronger genetic predisposition than EOAD.
source: It can be divided into two types: early-onset AD (EOAD, age of onset ≤65 years) and late-onset AD (LOAD, age of onset >65 years); the proportion of LOAD in patients with AD is approximately 95%, with LOAD having a stronger genetic predisposition than EOAD (Godyń et al., 2016; Ransohoff and El Khoury, 2015; Zou et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites published literature to support this claim.

claim: The population with AD is currently over 50 million worldwide.
source: According to the latest data from the World Health Organization (WHO), the population with AD is currently over 50 million worldwide and is expected to rise to 115 million by 2050 (GBD and Dementia Forecasting Collaborators, 2019; Anonymous, 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites WHO data and published literature to support this epidemiological claim.

claim: The population with AD is expected to rise to 115 million by 2050.

claim: Serological parameters such as C-reactive protein, lipids, and vitamin levels have been previously reported as potential biomarkers for AD.

claim: Factors related to lifestyle, family history, education, economic level, and environment correlate with AD.

claim: Most epidemiological studies are insufficient to draw definitive conclusions on causal association due to the potential for reverse causality and confounding bias.
source: However, most epidemiological studies are insufficient to draw definitive conclusions on causal association due to the potential for reverse causality and confounding bias.

claim: MR analysis reduces confounding and reverse causality due to the segregation and independent assortment of genes passed from parents to offspring.

claim: In the absence of pleiotropy and demographic stratification, MR can present a clear estimate of risk of the disease.
